title: How do barcodes work? The stripes are a shortcut
description: A supermarket barcode usually identifies the product, not its price. Discover how the bars and spaces become a number, and why two bottles can share a code.

sources.name: GS1 — How do GS1 GTINs and barcodes work?
GS1 — Are the description and price of the item included in the barcode?

sections.title: From stripes to a number
sections.html:
A barcode works by turning a pattern of bars and spaces into information a scanner can read. On ordinary supermarket packaging, that information is usually a product identification number.

It is a shortcut for the till: recognise the pattern, read the number, find the product. The checkout beep makes a very quick introduction.

sections.title: The spaces count too
sections.html:
Both the bars and the gaps matter. Their pattern gives the scanner something to decode. GS1 explains how the familiar retail barcode represents a GTIN, short for Global Trade Item Number.

The digits printed underneath are a human-readable version of that identifier. The stripes are there for the scanner; the number gives people another way to read it.

sections.title: So where is the price?
sections.html:
GS1 says the description and price are generally retrieved from a database. The barcode usually points to that information rather than carrying a tiny price list.

There are exceptions, including specialist codes for goods sold by variable weight and some coupons. So “barcodes never contain prices” would take the idea too far.

sections.title: Two bottles can share a code
sections.html:
Two identical bottles of the same drink and size can carry the same GTIN. It identifies the product type, not a unique personal name for every bottle.

For more clever things hiding in plain sight, discover how a zip joins its teeth and why a pen needs a tiny ball.
